This page goes with **Chapter 3, Minor Scales and Key Signatures** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/MinorScalesAndKeySignatures.html).

**You already know this.** You sing in minor with **la** as the resting tone (movable do, la-based minor; Gordon 105), you sing
harmonic minor with the raised **si** (Gordon 70), and you read both from the do signature. This chapter names what you already
do. La-based minor gives you a head start: the book's "relative minor" is the minor you've always sung.

Press ▶ to hear an example, or **▶ Sing** to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.

## What you know → what the book calls it

| You say (MLT) | The book says (Hutchinson ch. 3) |
|---|---|
| la, the resting tone in minor | tonic of the minor key, 1̂ |
| la ti do re mi fa so la | natural minor scale (Gordon: Aeolian tonality) |
| the same notes with si for so | harmonic minor scale (Gordon: harmonic minor tonality) |
| the do signature, resting on la | the minor key signature: "A minor" |
| major and minor with the same do signature | relative keys |
| the same tonic letter, major and minor | parallel keys |

## 3.1 Three kinds of minor

[Read 3.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/MinorScales.html)

**Natural minor** is la to la with no changes, the notes of the do signature from la. You've sung it as the minor of folk tunes and
of Gordon's Aeolian tonality.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="90"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Natural minor on A: la to la
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:Am
A, B, C D | E F G A |]
w:la ti do re mi fa so la
</script></div>

**Harmonic minor** raises so to **si**, so the scale has a half step into la like the half step ti–do in major. That's the
dominant sound you sing in harmonic minor patterns such as *mi si ti re* (Gordon 100). The book shows it as an accidental: in A minor,
G becomes G♯.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="90"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Harmonic minor on A: so becomes si (G♯)
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:Am
A, B, C D | E F ^G A |]
w:la ti do re mi fa si la
</script></div>

**Melodic minor** raises both fa and so on the way up, and goes back to natural minor on the way down. This one may be new: you have
the sound of si, but probably not of the raised fa. In movable do, raised fa is usually sung **fi** *(the syllable is common practice,
not yet checked against an MLT source)*.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="90"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Melodic minor on A: up with fi and si, down natural
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:Am
A, B, C D | E ^F ^G A | =G =F E D | C B, A,2 |]
w:la ti do re mi fi si la so fa mi re do ti la
</script></div>

**Where the book and MLT differ.** The book treats natural, harmonic and melodic minor as three forms of one minor key. Gordon treats
harmonic minor and Aeolian as two different **tonalities**, each with its own characteristic patterns (Gordon 149). Both see the
same notes; Gordon names what you hear, the book names what is written.

## 3.2 Minor key signatures: the same do signature

[Read 3.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/MinorKeySignatures.html)

You already read a do signature and rest on la. The book calls that key "the relative minor":

- **Find do, then go down to la** (two letters down, or up six). One sharp: do is G, la is E → **E minor**. Three flats: do is E♭,
  la is C → **C minor**.
- **Relative keys** share a signature: C major and A minor, G major and E minor. In MLT terms they share a do signature, with
  different resting tones (Gordon 155–156).
- **Parallel keys** share a tonic letter: A major and A minor. In MLT terms, do moves: A major has do on A; A minor has la on A, so do
  is on C.

The same tune, on the same do signature, ends on do (major) or la (minor):

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:No sharps or flats, resting on do: C major
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C E G E | F D B, C |]
w:do mi so mi fa re ti do
</script></div>

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:No sharps or flats, resting on la: A minor
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:Am
A, C E C | D B, ^G, A, |]
w:la do mi do re ti si la
</script></div>

**The harmonic minor accidental isn't in the signature.** Si is always written in the music. That's why C minor's signature is three
flats, but its scale needs a B♮.

## 3.3 Scale degree names in minor

[Read 3.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ScaleDegreeNames.html)

The book numbers minor from its own tonic, so **la is 1̂**. The names are the ones from [major](major-scales.qmd), with one
change: **so** (a whole step below la) is the **subtonic**, and **si** (a half step below) is the **leading tone**, as ti is in major.

| Syllable | Degree | Name |
|---|---|---|
| la | 1̂ | tonic |
| ti | 2̂ | supertonic |
| do | 3̂ | mediant |
| re | 4̂ | subdominant |
| mi | 5̂ | dominant |
| fa | 6̂ | submediant |
| so / si | 7̂ | subtonic / leading tone |

So "the dominant" in minor is **mi**, the note your harmonic minor dominant patterns start on.

## Bridging: from la to the book's names

1. **Find do, then la.** Say both letters: "do is B♭, la is G: G minor."
2. **Sing la to la**, then again on letters. That's natural minor.
3. **Swap in si**: raise the letter under so with a sharp or natural. That's harmonic minor.
4. **Parallel key?** Keep the tonic letter, move do: G major has do on G (one sharp); G minor has la on G (do on B♭, two flats).

## Check yourself

1. Two sharps. What is the relative minor?
2. In D minor, what letter is si?
3. In E minor harmonic, which note gets an accidental?
4. What is the parallel minor of E♭ major, and its signature?
5. In minor, which syllable is the dominant, 5̂?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. B minor (do is D, la is B).
2. C♯.
3. D becomes D♯ (so → si).
4. E♭ minor, six flats (la on E♭, so do is on G♭).
5. Mi.
:::
